raw_case_text: A 57-year-old male agricultural worker with a history of type 2 diabetes and arterial hypertension, presented with high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia and vomiting during the eight days prior to admission to our hospital. On the 8th day, he presented with psychomotor agitation, behavioral changes and seizures. A computed tomography (CT) brain scan without contrast was performed and had no abnormalities. CSF analysis presented neutrophilia (72%) pleocytosis (240 cells/mm) with normal glucose and high protein levels. Because of the neurological deterioration, the patient was admitted to our hospital. On admission, hypotension, bradycardia and a reduced level of conscience was observed (Glasgow coma scale 11). On the same day, the patient presented severe dyspnea and was promptly intubated. He received mechanical ventilation and continuous sedation. One-gram ceftriaxone and antiepileptic drugs were initiated. Laboratory tests revealed renal dysfunction, but conservative treatment (no hemodialysis) was maintained. On the second day, the antimicrobial therapy was modified to include one-gram of ampicillin and 250 mg of acyclovir. A brain MRI revealed frontal, parietal and mesial bilateral temporal cortical and subcortical altered signals with restricted diffusion and similar abnormalities in the posterior thalamus, midbrain and cerebellar vermis, and no enhancement was noted. These findings were compatible with a diffuse encephalitis. Further CSF analysis (day 12 of the disease) revealed pleocytosis (98 cells/mm with 68% of lymphocytes and 12% of monocytes), high protein (161 mg%), normal glucose (81 mg%) and high adenosine deaminase level (47.9 international units (UI)/L, normal < 4.5 UI/L). Negative results were obtained for syphilis and the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes virus types 1 and 2 were carried out. CSF and serum were positive for IgM antibodies to CHIKV (using the IgM antibody capture ELISA [MAC-ELISA] and commercial ELISA [Euroimmun, Lubeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany], respectively). A clinical deterioration of the patient was identified and despite the absence of sedative drugs, he remained in a coma and died on day 24 after onset of the illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male agricultural worker presented with an 8-day history of high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia, and vomiting, complicated on day 8 by acute psychomotor agitation, behavioral changes, and seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia, and vomiting for 8 days prior to admission. On the 8th day of illness, he developed psychomotor agitation, behavioral changes, and seizures; initial pre-transfer noncontrast brain CT was normal and lumbar puncture showed neutrophilic pleocytosis, prompting referral to our hospital where he presented with hypotension, bradycardia, reduced consciousness (GCS 11), and severe dyspnea requiring immediate endotracheal intubation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension; employed as an agricultural worker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia, vomiting, agitation, behavioral changes, seizures, reduced consciousness, and severe dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: hypotension, bradycardia, reduced level of consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 11, and severe dyspnea requiring immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation. Subsequently progressed to persistent coma.
objective.routine_investigations: Renal function panel: renal dysfunction (managed conservatively without hemodialysis). Serological testing for syphilis and HIV antibodies: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial noncontrast brain CT (day 8): normal. Initial CSF analysis (day 8): pleocytosis of 240 cells/mm3 (72% neutrophils), elevated protein, and normal glucose. Brain MRI (during hospitalization): altered cortical and subcortical signal intensities with restricted diffusion in the frontal, parietal, and bilateral mesial temporal lobes, posterior thalamus, midbrain, and cerebellar vermis without contrast enhancement, consistent with diffuse encephalitis. Repeat CSF analysis (day 12): pleocytosis of 98 cells/mm3 (68% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes), elevated protein 161 mg/dL, normal glucose 81 mg/dL, and markedly elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA) of 47.9 IU/L (reference <4.5 IU/L); CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, HSV-1, and HSV-2 negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal acute chikungunya virus (CHIKV) diffuse meningoencephalitis complicated by acute kidney injury and coma. Bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, HSV-1/2 encephalitis, neurosyphilis, and HIV were excluded. Confirmation: Positive anti-CHIKV IgM antibodies detected in both CSF (by MAC-ELISA) and serum (by Euroimmun commercial ELISA), alongside diffuse encephalitic changes on brain MRI. Management and outcome: Managed with mechanical ventilation, continuous sedation, antiepileptic drugs, conservative renal management, and empiric IV ceftriaxone (1 g), followed on day 2 by IV ampicillin (1 g) and acyclovir (250 mg). Despite supportive care and cessation of sedatives, the patient remained comatose and died on day 24 of illness.
